solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Functional line penned by American President of yesteryear

indicators.note: something penned by others is shut inside them, as in a pen, so the line goes within the president

parts.note: Abe (Abraham Lincoln) is a US president of long ago

explanation.surface: A historical note about some practical remark written by a long-dead American president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'President of yesteryear' is Abraham Lincoln, known as Honest Abe.
explanation.definitionFit: Something functional works and can be put to use, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Viewing all aspects brings alarm — choose to hide

indicators.note: the alarm word hides the choose word, holding it out of sight inside itself

parts.note: panic is sudden alarm
to opt is to choose

explanation.surface: A survey seeing everything at once alarms someone, who decides to go into hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: A panoptic view takes in everything at once, from the Greek for all-seeing.

clue.text: Walker in Liverpool, say, creating hostility when blocking main road

indicators.note: the hostility word blocks the road by sitting in the middle of it

parts.note: an artery is a major road
gall here is bitter feeling, rancour

explanation.surface: Someone walking in Liverpool grows angry when a main road is blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walker' looks like a pedestrian, but the Walker is a famous art museum in Liverpool; 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Walker in Liverpool is an example of a public picture museum, hence the 'say'.

clue.text: People who fulfil your wishes, a bit twisted inside?

definitions.text: People who fulfil your wishes, a bit twisted inside?

indicators.note: a small piece inside the word is turned about, so two neighbouring letters in the middle swap places

parts.note: compliers are people who comply with what you want

explanation.surface: A wry look at those who do as you ask yet are slightly warped within.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the L and I inside COMPLIERS gives the answer; the whole clue also describes crossword setters, who satisfy solvers and have devious minds.
explanation.definitionFit: Setters of puzzles serve solvers' wishes while being devious at heart, so the whole clue describes them.

clue.text: Hebrew character right out of bed

indicators.note: the right letter comes out of the bed word, leaving the rest

parts.note: a berth is a bed on a ship or train

explanation.surface: A Hebrew person jumps straight out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like a person, but it means a letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Beth is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a letter being a written character.

clue.text: Dress to sag

definitions.meaning: in military drill, to dress is to line up in ranks, which is the parade-ground order to form up
a roof that sags may collapse inwards, give way

explanation.surface: A garment that droops.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers form up in lines on command, and a structure that collapses inwards gives way; the phrase covers both.

clue.text: One appreciates the beautiful article following Society in a summer abroad

indicators.note: the society and article go in the French summer word

parts.note: ete is French for summer

indicators.note: the article comes after the society letter

parts.note: the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A lover of beauty reads an article about society while on holiday abroad one summer.
explanation.walkthrough: STHE goes inside ETE, after its first E, and A comes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An aesthete is a person devoted to art and beauty, someone with refined taste.

clue.text: Bird box in front of terraced houses?

indicators.note: the box word comes before the houses word

parts.note: to spar is to box
a row is a line of terraced houses

explanation.surface: A nesting box hung on the front of a row of terraced houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a nesting box, but it is the verb, to fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparrow is a common small bird, an example of the class.

clue.text: Man of power, wouldn't you say, in speech?

indicators.note: spoken out, the word sounds like the one wanted

parts.note: a speaker adds a 'what?' at the end of a remark, as in 'jolly good, what?', asking agreement

explanation.surface: A rhetorical tag about a powerful man, put to the listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What?' as a tag question, old-fashioned British upper-class speech, means 'wouldn't you say?'.
explanation.definitionFit: James Watt, the engineer, gave his name to the unit of power.

clue.text: Say, a cleric getting old, bent over, in twilight years?

indicators.note: bending a line of letters over turns it back on itself, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: e.g. means 'say', for example
Rev is short for Reverend, a cleric

explanation.surface: A clergyman growing old and stooped in his last years.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading EG + A + REV + O backwards gives O-VER-A-GE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone beyond the age limit is too old, which fits a person late in life, with a question mark for looseness.

clue.text: Trained ventriloquist once given a sort of monkey

parts.note: Peter Brough was a British radio ventriloquist of the 1950s, with the dummy Archie Andrews
a monkey is the heavy ram of a pile-driver, and a tup is such a ram or hammer head

explanation.surface: An old-time ventriloquist is given a monkey to train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey' looks like the animal, but it is the drop-hammer of a pile-driver, also called a tup.
explanation.definitionFit: A child brought up well has been reared and schooled, so the phrase means trained.

clue.text: The man with plot of ground is a serf

parts.note: he refers to a man
a lot is a plot of land

explanation.surface: A man working a small plot of land is a peasant bound to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A helot was a serf in ancient Sparta, so the word is a type of bonded labourer.

clue.text: Praise formerly accompanied by endless peal

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: the bell word loses its last letter, its end

parts.note: a toll is the ringing of a bell

explanation.surface: Praise once came with a long ringing of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Leave horrible people as soon as there's nothing to lose

parts.note: lice is slang for contemptible people

indicators.note: the word for 'as soon as' must lose the nothing letter

parts.note: once means as soon as
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Walk out on nasty people the moment you have nothing to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a verb but is the noun, permission.
explanation.definitionFit: Licence is permission or freedom to do something, the same as leave in 'by your leave'.

clue.text: Keep an eye on the old woman and man in a doomed situation

parts.note: to check is to monitor
ma is a mother, an 'old woman'
Ted is a man's name

explanation.surface: Watch over your mother and a man who are in a hopeless plight.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess a king checkmated is beaten for good, so the word means trapped with no escape.

clue.text: Country hospital is to be included in business arrangement

indicators.note: the hospital letter and is go within the country word

parts.note: France is a country

explanation.surface: A country's hospital joins a commercial deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A franchise is a licence to trade under another firm's name, a commercial deal.

clue.text: Greek character facing obvious fix, keeping on in place devoid of particular reaction

indicators.note: the Greek letter faces the obvious word, standing in front of it

parts.note: nu is the Greek letter N
clear means plain, obvious

indicators.note: the fix word keeps on inside it

parts.note: to freeze prices is to fix them

explanation.surface: A Greek holding an obvious fixed position in a place where nobody reacts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reaction' looks like a response, but here it is the nuclear chain reaction.
explanation.definitionFit: A zone banning atomic weapons or power is free of fission, the 'particular reaction'.

clue.text: Something must be denied by this philosopher

definitions.text: Something must be denied by this philosopher

parts.words: Something must be denied by this philosopher
parts.note: this thinker denies everything, so any 'something' at all is rejected; Latin nihil means nothing

explanation.surface: A philosopher must deny some proposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something' reads as 'a certain thing' but means anything that exists.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a philosopher rejects all values and beliefs, so whatever exists is denied.

clue.text: Certain society giving way to allow for public opening

indicators.note: the shortened certain word makes room for the public word to come before it

parts.note: overt means open, public

indicators.note: the society letter gives way, leaving the certain word

parts.note: sure means certain

explanation.surface: A sure society yields so the public can be let in to an opening.
explanation.definitionFit: An overture is the orchestral opening of an opera, or an opening approach.

clue.text: Bluff ruler that gets cold-hearted, appearing to be calm

indicators.note: the king and 'that' get the cold letter at their heart, the hyphenated '-hearted' placing it in the middle

parts.note: Bluff King Hal is a nickname of Henry VIII
yon is an old word for that

explanation.surface: A blunt king grows cold-hearted yet seems serene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bluff' looks like deceit, but bluff means hearty here, from 'Bluff King Hal' for Henry VIII.
explanation.definitionFit: Halcyon days are peaceful and tranquil, so the word means serene.

clue.text: Wreath laid on earth in European city

indicators.note: in a down clue the wreath sits on top of the earth word

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland
an earth is a fox's den

explanation.surface: A wreath laid on the ground in a European city.
explanation.definitionFit: Leiden is a university city in the Netherlands.

clue.text: This massage is said to be requirement

indicators.note: said marks a word heard, sounding like the requirement word

parts.note: a need is a requirement

explanation.surface: A massage claimed to be essential.
explanation.definitionFit: To knead is to work muscles with the hands, which is massaging.

clue.text: Fearless lover spending pounds

indicators.note: spending the pounds means the pounds letter goes

parts.note: a darling is a sweetheart
L (librae) is the sign for pounds sterling

explanation.surface: A bold lover is splashing out money.
explanation.definitionFit: Daring means bold and brave, a direct adjective synonym.

clue.text: Supports made from alloy crumbling away at the bottom

indicators.note: the alloy loses its last letter, the bottom in a down clue

parts.note: brass is an alloy of copper and zinc

explanation.surface: Supports made from a metal that is crumbling at its base.
explanation.definitionFit: A bra is a supporting undergarment, so the plural means supports.

clue.text: A part of Edinburgh Castle, I think — only a part

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Someone guesses that the Castle forms part of Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Leith is the port district of Edinburgh, in the north of the city.

clue.text: Going off on a trip?

definitions.meaning: game meat that is going off smells strong, beginning to rot
someone on a drug trip is intoxicated

explanation.surface: Setting out on a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both tainted, of meat, and intoxicated by drugs.

clue.text: Fee rather bad — when to expect proper reward?!

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made bad, put into disorder

explanation.surface: A complaint that a fee is poor value, with true payment only coming later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fee' suggests payment, but the real reward is in the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Religious belief places just rewards in the afterlife, after death.

clue.text: Tops on radio vehicles

indicators.note: on the radio words are heard, not seen

parts.note: to top someone is slang for killing, to slay

explanation.surface: Radio chart toppers about vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleighs are sledges drawn over snow, and so a kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Something in suet that's nastier when chewed

indicators.note: chewing mashes the word up, so its letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Suet tastes nastier as you chew it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stearin is a fatty compound found in animal fats such as suet.
